items.title: Armand Hug Interview, 1960-07-14
items.q: But to get back to Buzzy helping me, he showed me quite a bit of things, quite a few tricks that I even started.

ctx.x: Yeah, he faked too. I don't know if he was a real jazz drummer, but I know he was quite an accomplished drummer. I would say that the turning point in my jazz career came when I met Buzzy Williams. Because my Uncle, Dewey Schmid, had a real good acquaintance with him. He knew him real well and told him that he would bring me and bring him out to the house and let me meet him. And I was about 11 years old or something like that, 12 at the time. I must say that Buzzy was really a wonderful person as he is today. He…
He showed you the tenth style bass, and that was way back, huh? That was, well, that was back about 1926.

items.title: Armand Hug Interview, 1965-09-13
items.q: I had one pianist around here by the name of Buzzy Williams, who was very, very excellent, and he gave me a lot of encouragement and a lot of help.

ctx.x: Well, certainly your piano style goes beyond the ragtime realm. What have any other pianists of the swing era or the modern era influence your playing as it's constituted today?

I think that the first real impact that hit me, when I say impact, I was already going under the influence of the old timers like Jelly Roll and the ragtime pianists. And I had one pianist around here by the name of Buzzy Williams, who was very, very excellent, and he gave me a lot of encouragement and a lot of help. But getting back to the other pianists, I would say that the first one that really had a terrific impact on me was Earl Hines. I think that he did more to revolutionize my style of playing probably…
Did you take up, were you taken up much by Art Tatum's style?
